questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A field biologist recalls plant names better at the original survey site; what is this?

options.misconception: confuses external context with internal state
confuses cue mismatch with trace loss

questions.explanation: Context-dependent memory improves recall when the retrieval environment matches the encoding environment. The original site provides matching contextual cues.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A field biologist recalls observations better when in the same mood as during the survey; what is this?

options.misconception: confuses internal state with external context
confuses state effects with prior learning interference
confuses state effects with source confusion

questions.explanation: State-dependent memory improves recall when the internal state at retrieval matches the state at encoding. Mood is an internal state.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A field biologist remembers the first species in a list best; which effect?

options.misconception: confuses first-item advantage with last-item advantage
confuses position effect with later interference
confuses position effect with prior interference

questions.explanation: The primacy effect gives better recall for early items, often due to greater rehearsal and transfer to long-term memory. The recency effect favors last items.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A field biologist remembers the last species in a list best; which effect?

options.misconception: confuses last-item advantage with first-item advantage
confuses position effect with internal state

questions.explanation: The recency effect gives better recall for the most recent items, typically because they remain in short-term memory. Primacy favors early items.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A field biologist's old survey labels disrupt recall of new labels; what is this?
questions.explanation: Proactive interference occurs when older learning disrupts recall of newer learning. Retroactive interference is the reverse, when new learning disrupts old.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A field biologist's new survey labels disrupt recall of old labels; what is this?
questions.explanation: Retroactive interference occurs when newer learning disrupts recall of older learning. Proactive interference is the reverse.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A field biologist's recall drops rapidly then levels off; what pattern?

options.text: Forgetting curve with rapid then slow loss

questions.explanation: The forgetting curve shows rapid initial loss of information followed by a slower decline. Ebbinghaus described this pattern.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A field biologist's unrehearsed notes fade without review; what explains the loss?
questions.explanation: Decay theory attributes forgetting to the fading of memory traces over time without rehearsal. Interference and context are alternative explanations.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A field biologist knows a species name but cannot produce it; what failed?

options.text: Storage, because the name was lost

options.misconception: confuses access failure with trace decay

questions.explanation: Retrieval failure occurs when stored information cannot be accessed. The trace may be intact but inaccessible due to missing cues.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A field biologist cannot recall a stressful survey event; what might explain it?

options.text: Decay of the trace over time

questions.explanation: Motivated forgetting suggests unpleasant memories may be suppressed or forgotten. Interference and decay are alternative, non-motivational explanations.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A field biologist's recall changes after hearing a misleading report; what is this?
questions.explanation: The misinformation effect occurs when misleading information alters memory of an event. Source amnesia involves forgetting where information came from.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A field biologist remembers a fact but not where it was learned; what is this?

options.misconception: confuses source loss with memory alteration
confuses source loss with access failure

questions.explanation: Source amnesia is remembering information while forgetting its origin. The misinformation effect alters the memory content itself.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A field biologist cannot recall events before an injury; what is this?

options.misconception: reverses the temporal direction of amnesia

questions.explanation: Retrograde amnesia is the inability to recall events before an injury or trauma. Anterograde amnesia is the inability to form new memories after it.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A field biologist cannot form new survey memories after an injury; what is this?

options.misconception: reverses the temporal direction of amnesia

questions.explanation: Anterograde amnesia is the inability to form new memories after an injury. Retrograde amnesia affects memories formed before the injury.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A field biologist recalls species better after self-testing than rereading; what is this?

options.misconception: confuses testing benefit with scheduling benefit

questions.explanation: The testing effect is improved retention from retrieving information, such as self-testing, rather than passive rereading.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A field biologist recalls better after study sessions spread over weeks; what is this?

options.misconception: confuses scheduling benefit with retrieval benefit

questions.explanation: The spacing effect is better retention when study sessions are distributed over time rather than massed. Testing effect involves retrieval practice.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A field biologist encodes findings in a forest; recall is best in?

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A field biologist encodes data while calm; recall improves when?
questions.explanation: State-dependent memory predicts better recall when the internal state at retrieval matches the state at encoding. Calm matches calm.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology

questions.stem: Why do early list items show better recall in a field survey?

options.text: They receive more rehearsal and transfer

options.misconception: confuses early items with recent items
attributes primacy solely to interference reduction

questions.explanation: Primacy is attributed to greater rehearsal and transfer to long-term memory for early items. Recency relies on short-term retention.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Why do last list items show better recall in a field survey?

options.misconception: confuses short-term retention with long-term transfer

questions.explanation: Recency is attributed to the last items remaining in short-term memory. Primacy relies on rehearsal and long-term transfer.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Old labels hurt new recall, while new labels hurt old recall; what pair?
questions.explanation: Old disrupting new is proactive interference; new disrupting old is retroactive interference. Direction determines the type.

questions.stem: A biologist recalls 80 percent after 1 day and 40 percent after 7 days; what is the drop in percentage points?

provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: Is motivated forgetting the best explanation for all forgotten unpleasant events?

options.text: Yes, unpleasant events are always suppressed
No, interference and decay also explain forgetting

questions.explanation: Motivated forgetting is one explanation, but interference and decay also explain forgetting. It is not the sole cause.

confuses source loss with pre-injury loss

provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Which amnesia affects memories formed before versus after an injury?
questions.explanation: Retrograde amnesia affects pre-injury memories; anterograde amnesia affects post-injury memory formation. Direction of time distinguishes them.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

Mood is context, environment is state

questions.explanation: Context refers to external environment; state refers to internal condition such as mood. Both can cue retrieval when matched.

questions.explanation: State-dependent memory benefits from matching states, but exact identity is not strictly required. Approximate matches can also aid retrieval.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A field biologist plots recall by list position; what shape?
questions.explanation: The serial position curve is U-shaped, with better recall for first and last items than middle items. Primacy and recency create the highs.

provenance.author: bank-team-psychology
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.stem: Is decay the only explanation for forgetting over time?

options.text: Yes, decay is the sole cause

questions.explanation: Decay theory attributes forgetting to trace fading, but interference theory attributes it to competing memories. Both are viable explanations.

confuses cue recovery with interference removal
assumes cue recovery means no prior encoding

questions.explanation: Recovery after a cue indicates the trace was intact but inaccessible, so retrieval failed rather than storage. Decay would not reverse so easily.

questions.stem: Motivated forgetting differs from decay in that it?

questions.stem: Can misinformation alter an original memory rather than just add to it?

options.text: No, original memory is always preserved
Yes, misinformation can alter the original
Yes, but only in sensory memory

questions.explanation: The misinformation effect can alter the original memory, not merely add new information. Source amnesia involves source confusion, not content change.

provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used
